To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

massive star-forming galaxies are likely to experience positive feedback conditions, in the sense that they are likely to retain most of the matter reprocessed by massive stars, and that they are not likely to be the sources of supergalactic winds, as previously suggested in the literature.

the interplay of the thermalization of stellar winds and supernova explosions, radiative cooling, and gravity determines the evolution of the gas returned to the assembling galaxy by massive stars, and that the resulting gas dynamics is likely to be bimodal, with mass accumulation and expulsion in different zones of the galaxy.
the interstellar medium of assembling galaxies is a complex dynamical system in which star formation and stellar feedback processes are strongly coupled.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental question in galaxy evolution: how does a starburst affect the surrounding interstellar medium?
the interplay between massive star formation and the gravitational potential of young assembling galaxies.
a detailed study of hydrodynamics of matter reinserted in young assembling galaxies via stellar winds and SNe explosions in massive stars.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
star formation in the most massive assembling galaxies at high redshift may be the main driver of the interstellar matter enrichment in the universe.
the extreme star formation feedback regime is the rule rather than the exception in the most massive assembling galaxies.

massive star formation in assembling galaxies is likely to be a positive feedback phenomenon, with little impact on the surrounding intergalactic medium, but with a significant impact on the interstellar medium of the host galaxy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the positive star formation feedback may be the dominant feedback mode in massive assembling galaxies, and that it may be responsible for the observed high metallicity in the interstellar matter of high redshift quasar hosts.
the extreme positive feedback regime in star formation may be a common phenomenon in the most massive star-forming regions in the Universe.

the positive star formation feedback regime is likely to take place in massive assembling galaxies at high redshifts, while the negative star formation feedback regime (in which the mechanical energy injected by massive stars is sufficient to prevent the formation of new stars in the assembling galaxy) would occur in the local Universe.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, contrary to the common belief, star formation feedback may not be the main driver of galaxy evolution in the most active star forming systems.
the star formation feedback condition in assembling galaxies is a function of the mass of the host galaxy and the mechanical luminosity of massive stars.
the interplay of gravity and hydrodynamics in star-forming regions can have a profound influence on the evolution of the interstellar medium and the star formation history of the host galaxy.
